title: Bayes’ rule and base rates
summary: Turn a test’s accuracy into the chance a positive result is real, and see why rare events mislead.
intro: **Bayes’ rule** updates a prior belief P(D) with evidence. For a positive test, P(D | +) = P(+ | D) P(D) / P(+).
The denominator adds both ways of testing positive: true positives, sensitivity × prior, and false positives, false-positive rate × (1 − prior).

When the condition is rare, false positives from the large healthy group can swamp the true ones. The same arithmetic explains why a fraud or anomaly model with 99% recall can still have low precision.
formula: P(D | +) = s·p / (s·p + f·(1 − p))     p = prior, s = sensitivity, f = false-positive rate
prompt: Write `posterior(prior, sensitivity, false_positive_rate)` that returns P(condition | positive test).
hints: Work out the true-positive mass, sensitivity × prior.
Then the false-positive mass, false-positive rate × (1 − prior).
The answer is the true share of all positives.
explanation: Out of 10,000 people with a 1% prior, 100 have the condition and 99 of them test positive. Of the 9,900 without it, 5% (495) also test positive. So only 99 of 594 positives are real: 1/6, about 17%. With a 50% prior the same test is right 90% of the time.

diagram.title: Who tests positive, out of 10,000 people
diagram.alt: Bar chart of 10,000 people tested with a 1 percent prior, 99 percent sensitivity and 5 percent false-positive rate: 99 true positives against 495 false positives.
diagram.caption: False positives from the large healthy group outnumber true positives five to one, so a positive result is real only about 17% of the time.
